say.text: Before we teach the airway, try a harder one. Make your call, and we will work through it after.

A 40-year-old cyclist was knocked off by a van. At the scene he spoke clearly to the crew. Now, in your bay, he is hoarse, with a swelling growing under his jaw and noisy breathing. What is your next move?

choices.label: Reassess the airway now, and prepare a definitive airway
He spoke clearly, so carry on with the survey
A hoarse voice only: analgesia, then the secondary survey
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a swelling in the neck does to the airway over the next few minutes, not what he said at the scene.
Yes. A changing voice and a growing neck swelling mean the airway may close, so you reassess it at once and get ready for a definitive airway.
That choice is not right. Clear speech at the scene feels like proof the airway is fine, so the survey seems finished.
Speech showed the airway was open for the moment. The airway is changing now, and that is what you are deciding on.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the word moment. Speech is a snapshot, and a hoarse voice is one of the signs that the airway is changing.

say.text: That choice is not right. A hoarse voice sounds like a minor complaint, so treating the pain and moving on looks like the next job.
A changing voice with a swelling in the neck is one of the signs of airway compromise.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a hoarse voice is an early airway sign, not a side complaint.

say.text: You picked to carry on. That reads the speech from the scene as if it still described the airway now.
Reassess the airway whenever the patient deteriorates. A neck haematoma can close the airway, so the airway decides the next step, not what he said earlier.
You picked analgesia and the secondary survey. That treats the voice and leaves the airway unchecked.
Look at the airway again now, and get ready for a definitive airway if it is failing.
The airway can change in minutes. Speech proves it was open at that moment, not that it will stay open.
Hoarseness, noisy breathing and a growing neck swelling are signs of compromise. A neck haematoma can obstruct the airway, which makes a definitive airway the indication.
A different patient. A man was talking at the scene. Now in the ambulance his GCS has fallen to 7 and he is not protecting his airway.
What decides the airway now?

choices.label: He moved his limbs earlier, so the airway is safe
GCS of 8 or less, which means he cannot protect it
Wait for a head CT before deciding on the tube
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Which measure in the stem is a score you can track, and what number does the rule use?
Yes. A GCS of 8 or less is the indication for a definitive airway, because the patient can no longer protect his own.
That choice is not right. Movement at the scene feels like a sign that the brain and airway are working, so the score seems less important.
Movement is a snapshot. The GCS is the measure that sets the airway trigger.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what each finding measures: movement is an early sign, but the rule that decides the airway is the GCS.

say.text: You picked the reassuring movement. That turns one sign into an all-clear.
A GCS of 8 or less is an indication for a definitive airway, and a patient at that level cannot protect the airway.
Tempting, because a head scan feels like the thorough next step. The airway decision is made on the GCS, and imaging can follow it.
In an unconscious patient the airway most often fails because the tongue falls back against the pharynx. Snoring and gurgling are the warning signs.
Open the airway with a jaw thrust and keep the neck still, because the cervical spine is assumed injured. A definitive airway is a tube in the trachea with the cuff below the cords.
A 9-year-old was pulled from a house fire with burns to the face. Two intubation attempts have failed, and the saturation is falling.
Which emergency airway do you use?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy, the usual adult emergency airway
Emergency tracheostomy, as a definitive surgical airway
Needle cricothyroidotomy with jet oxygenation for now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about the age in the stem: what does a child's cricoid cartilage need to stay intact?
Yes. Under 12, the emergency route is a needle, because the cricoid cartilage must not be cut in a child.
It is temporary: oxygenation lasts only about 30 to 45 minutes, so a definitive airway must follow.
That choice is not right. The adult rule feels like the safe default in a failed airway, and nothing in the stem flags a change.
The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring supporting the upper trachea, and cutting it in a child risks lasting damage.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is the adult rule carried over without checking the age. Check the age before you choose.

say.text: Tempting, because a tracheostomy is a definitive airway and it sounds like a planned surgical route.
In an emergency it is slower and bleeds more than a cricothyroidotomy, so it is not the quick rescue this child needs.
You picked the adult surgical airway. The age in the stem changes the rule.
Adults get the surgical cricothyroidotomy. Under 12, the cricoid is the one ring to keep intact, so a needle is used.
Adults: surgical cricothyroidotomy is the emergency airway of choice, with the cut made through the cricothyroid membrane.
Under 12: avoid the surgical cut and use a needle cricothyroidotomy, which is temporary and gives oxygen for about 30 to 45 minutes.
The same failed airway, cannot intubate and cannot oxygenate, in two patients: a 35-year-old and a 9-year-old.
Which pair of emergency airways fits?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy for both patients, to be safe
Needle cricothyroidotomy for both, since it is quicker
Surgical for the adult, needle for the child
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Take the two patients one at a time, and ask what the age changes about the cut.
Yes. The adult gets the surgical cricothyroidotomy, and the child gets the needle, because a child's cricoid cartilage must not be cut.
That choice is not right. One rule for both patients feels simpler and safer, and the adult surgical airway is the one you learned first.
The adult can take a surgical cut, but the cricoid ring of a child must not be cut.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is one rule for two patients. The age is the qualifier that splits them.

say.text: You picked one rule for both. The adult and the child differ at 12, so each gets its own airway.
The surgical cut is for adults; the needle is the child's temporary airway.
Tempting, because the needle is the quick rescue and seems to fit any failed airway.
A needle only bridges oxygen for a short time, and the adult still gets a surgical airway.
